query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a conformal, ultrathin nickel coating on tungsten particles prior to copper infiltration will improve interfacial bonding and reduce void formation relative to current vapor‐coated tungsten powders, thereby producing a more uniform and mechanically robust W–Cu composite for fusion-reactor heat-transfer joints.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composites fabricated from uncoated or vapor‐coated tungsten particles sintered with copper, which show phase separation and voids leading to impaired thermal transport.
generation.intervention: Apply a uniform, ultrathin nickel coating (via techniques like chemical vapor deposition or electroplating) to tungsten particles before subsequent Cu infiltration/sintering.
generation.conditions: The tungsten particles are coated, then mixed with Cu powder or subjected to Cu infiltration under a controlled atmosphere, with sintering/infiltration performed at a moderate temperature (e.g., ~1200°C) and under reduced pressure or inert gas to minimize oxidation. Post‐processing, the composite is exposed to irradiation and high thermal flux conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints.
generation.structural_mediator: The nickel interlayer at the W/Cu interface facilitates improved wetting and diffusion bonding between tungsten and copper while acting as a diffusion barrier to prevent interfacial reactions leading to void formation.
generation.mechanism: The Ni coating lowers the interfacial energy and improves the wettability of molten or sintered Cu on tungsten surfaces. This enhanced bonding minimizes the formation of voids and phase separation by promoting more uniform interdiffusion and contact during the infiltration/sintering process. It also serves as a barrier that stabilizes the interface under irradiation, thereby preserving mechanical durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline fabricated by vapor coating and sintering of tungsten particles in Cu, the Ni-coated tungsten approach is expected to yield a composite with significantly reduced void content and improved thermal conductivity, while maintaining or enhancing mechanical durability under irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: Existing fabrication protocols such as vapor coating tungsten powders followed by sintering, spark-plasma sintering, or mechanical alloying that suffer from residual voids and imperfect interfacial contact.
generation.boundary: This intervention is anticipated to be effective for composites produced under the moderate temperature (sub-1200°C) infiltration/sintering conditions and tested under high thermal flux and irradiation similar to fusion-reactor environments. Scaling to larger or more complex geometries and long-term service exposures remain to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement in interfacial integrity and thermal transport is uncertain, and there is risk of Ni diffusion into the Cu or W phases over prolonged irradiation that may modify the interfacial properties. The uniformity and adhesion quality of the Ni coating over complex tungsten geometries also need further verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one using conventional vapor-coated tungsten powders and another using tungsten powders pre-coated with an ultrathin Ni layer. Both sets will undergo identical Cu infiltration/sintering processes under inert atmosphere at ~1200°C. The microstructure, including interface quality and void content, will be characterized using SEM, TEM, and X-ray tomography. Thermal conductivity will be measured via laser flash analysis, and mechanical durability will be assessed through high-temperature cyclic loading and irradiation exposure tests mimicking fusion-reactor conditions.
measurements: Void content and distribution at the W/Cu interface (via SEM/TEM/X-ray tomography)
Interfacial diffusion profiles (using EDS or atom probe tomography)
Thermal conductivity values (using laser flash analysis)
Mechanical integrity and durability under cyclic thermal and irradiation conditions (via mechanical testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in void formation and improvement in thermal conductivity and mechanical durability compared to the conventional vapor-coated samples, then the hypothesis that the Ni coating intervention overcomes the fabrication limitations is falsified.
